title: Continental tent stitch
subtitle: The diagonal covering stitch that works in rows across canvas
excerpt: Continental tent stitch covers needlepoint canvas with a single diagonal stitch per hole, worked row by row. It is the quickest path to full coverage and the right starting point for most charted needlepoint.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), canvaswork chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), tent stitch entry. Weldon's Practical Needlework, canvaswork series (1887).

glossaryTerms.definition: A diagonal stitch worked over one canvas intersection, travelling from lower left to upper right. Rows progress horizontally; the needle re-enters the canvas at the next position to the left on the return pass.
The point on needlepoint canvas where a horizontal thread and a vertical thread cross. Each intersection is one stitch position.
Mono canvas with 13 holes per 2.5 cm. A standard weight suitable for most needlepoint projects and compatible with one strand of Persian wool or two strands of tapestry wool.

content.text: Continental tent stitch
covers each
canvas intersection

with one diagonal stitch running from lower left to upper right. The needle travels down and across the back of the canvas to reach the next position. The result is a diagonal texture on the front and a slanted brick-work pattern on the back.
Continental pulls the canvas slightly off-square because every stitch crosses in the same direction. For small pieces, this distortion is manageable. For larger pieces, stretch on a
scroll frame
and block when finished.
Work in natural or bright task light. Counting errors on canvas are difficult to unpick without distorting the threads.
What you need

items.label: Canvas
items.value: 13-count mono canvas, cut at least 5 cm larger than the finished design on every side

items.label: Thread
items.value: One strand of Persian wool, or two strands of tapestry wool — both suit 13-count

items.label: Needle
items.value: Tapestry size 20 — blunt tip, eye large enough for the thread to feed without forcing

items.label: Frame
items.value: Scroll frame or slate frame to keep the canvas square while you work

content.text: How to work continental tent stitch

Thread the needle with one strand of Persian wool, about 45 cm long. Start by tucking the tail under the first few stitches on the back as you work, or use an away-knot placed a few centimetres from your first stitch.
Bring the needle up through the canvas at the lower left of the first intersection you want to cover. This is position 1.
Insert the needle at the upper right corner of the same intersection. This is position 2. You have placed one diagonal stitch over one canvas intersection.
Bring the needle back up at the lower left of the next intersection to the right, position 3, by passing under the canvas. Continue across the row, placing one stitch at each intersection.
At the end of the row, turn the canvas and work the return row in the same way. The stitches on the front all run in the same direction.
When the thread runs short, finish by running the tail under five or six completed stitches on the back before cutting. Never knot the end where it will sit under a stitch.
Strand count for 13-count canvas
On
13-count canvas

use one strand of Persian wool (which separates into three and you use one), or two strands of tapestry wool. The canvas threads should just barely show between stitches on the first stitch; the second stitch laid alongside it should lock the canvas solid. If threads bunch or are hard to pull through, the strand count is too heavy for the canvas count.

items.cause: All stitches running diagonally in one direction create cumulative tension.
items.fix: Mount the canvas on a scroll frame before starting. Block the finished piece by wetting and pinning to a board cut square before it dries.

items.cause: The stitch motion gradually spins the thread in one direction.
items.fix: Every few stitches, let the needle hang freely and allow the thread to untwist under its own weight.

items.cause: Thread too thin for the canvas count, or insufficient strand count.
items.fix: Add a strand. On 13-count canvas, one strand of Persian wool is the minimum; two strands of tapestry wool give fuller coverage.

content.text: What continental underpins
Continental tent is the foundation of most charted needlepoint. Once it is comfortable, the next step is
basketweave tent stitch
, which distributes tension better on large fills and is the standard for background areas.
